tagline: An AI-designed antibody sandwich assay for blood neurofilament light chain, for cheap non-invasive early screening of neurodegenerative disease
summary: BAID-China built Neurofilux, a blood test for neurofilament light chain (NfL), a biomarker of neuronal damage that rises years before Alzheimer's or ALS symptoms appear but is currently detectable only by expensive, invasive or insufficiently sensitive methods. They expressed the NfL rod domain (residues 93-396) as antigen, used the generative model RFantibody to design candidate antibodies, screened them with a multi-objective scoring pipeline, validated eight candidates experimentally and found two pairs outperforming commercial antibodies in sandwich ELISA, then converted the validated antibodies into nanobodies for stability and cost. Their inclusivity work is organised around a self-defined 3A framework - Adaptation, Awareness, Accessibility - and centres on a tactile magnetic genetic-circuit kit for blind children, developed in two phases and donated to a school for the visually impaired.

dry.frameworks: Self-defined 3A inclusivity framework (Adaptation: convert visually-presented science into tactile, auditory and interactive forms; Awareness: dispel stereotypes and spread barrier-free science; Accessibility: remove visual, language and technical thresholds), with every activity required to map onto at least one dimension. Grounded in a literature review citing Hayes and Proulx (2023) on barriers for visually impaired science students and CAST (2024) Universal Design for Learning, plus Design Thinking, Empathy Mapping and Universal Design concepts taught by an invited expert. Accessibility work was benchmarked against WCAG.
dry.dataviz: All wiki charts redrawn in the eight-colour Okabe-Ito colour-blind-safe palette, chosen because each colour keeps enough luminance difference to stay readable in greyscale; the team published a colour-blindness simulation figure verifying that elements remain distinguishable under red-green, blue-yellow and total colour-blindness simulation.
dry.datascience: Multi-objective computational scoring to rank AI-generated antibody candidates by predicted sensitivity; comparative legal and building-code research across China, Egypt, Pakistan and the United States compiled into an open-access international accessibility database; pre-activity knowledge survey of junior and senior high school students on neurodegenerative disease awareness.
dry.software: RFantibody generative AI model used for de novo antibody design, followed by computational screening and virtual validation of nanobody conversions; a laboratory accessibility audit tool and evaluation form built on universal design principles; a wiki accessibility plugin offering a five-step text magnifier, a language switcher and one-click return-to-top, with semantic HTML restructured so screen readers can parse the navigation hierarchy.

good.publicEngagement: BAID-China started from evidence rather than instinct: a literature review on STEM barriers for disabled students (high lab benches, reading instrument data, observing phenomena, the need for written or sign-language support) plus a field visit to Bethel China, a charity for preschool children with visual impairments, where they identified two concrete problems - classes run with several children to one teacher, which blocks understanding, and tactile picture books that deliver touch sensation but almost no actual knowledge content. Both findings set the agenda. First strand: a team member, Audrey, joined the iGEM community project 'Accessibility in Synbio Labs' at the iGEM Annual Community Day in early 2026 and led BAID-China's inclusivity group through Phase 1 (research and database development) and Phase 2 (lab audits) alongside iGEM members from China, Egypt, Pakistan and the United States. With team Concordia-Shanghai they researched China's Accessibility Environment Construction Law, the Law on the Protection of Persons with Disabilities and GB 55019-2021 General Specifications for Accessibility in Architecture and Municipal Engineering, focusing on doorway clearance and wheelchair turning diameter, and the national research sets were compiled into an open-access comparative international database. The audit tool was then reviewed by Chloe Franklin, a scientist who uses a wheelchair, whose feedback changed it substantially: replace the Yes/No/N/A format with a scale that reflects degrees of accessibility because wheelchair users' needs differ widely; add specific measurable criteria with dimensional requirements; and weight audit items by importance, since building entrances, elevators, emergency evacuation routes and restrooms are foundational while equipment height and storage can be adjusted more easily. The team logged her suggestions, took them to weekly meetings, produced a new version, and credits co-creators by name (Sami from Team Toronto 2026, Mohamed, Sophie and Linda). They are honest that pilot testing was not completed within the season and commit to continuing next year. Second strand, and the signature contribution: Chloe Franklin's remark that a beautiful accessible lab on a high floor of a building with no accessible elevator is meaningless pushed the team from physical access to information access. They built a tactile magnetic genetic-circuit kit in which each component is a distinct shape rather than a colour or diagram: two circles of different sizes for input signals (large = normal cell, small = cancer cell), a star for an activator, an X for a repressor, an arrow for a promoter, a rectangle for a gene, a semicircle for a terminator and a pentagon for the output (anticancer drug release). This was embedded in a 45-minute workshop of four activities, run five times for more than 110 participants in total. Activity One sent sighted participants into the team's own laboratory in a wheelchair, where they discovered the doorway was barely wider than the chair, a slope and uneven bricks blocked independent movement, and bench spacing left no turning room. Activity Two brought in David Doyle, Project Head of the Accessibility in Synbio Labs community project, to teach Design Thinking, Empathy Mapping and Universal Design - the point being that environments should be designed around users rather than users adapting to environments. Activity Three recreated a standard Chinese middle-school microscope exercise, but half the participants were denied visual access: one student described cell shapes, features and spatial arrangement in words while the others had to reconstruct the specimen on paper, which reliably failed, demonstrating that people can sit in the same classroom and receive very different amounts of information. Activity Four had blindfolded participants assemble, by touch alone, a circuit that releases a drug when cancer cells are detected but not when normal cells are present. Phase 1 feedback exposed real design flaws - unclear verbal instructions about logical relationships between blocks, and block shapes and sizes that were hard to grasp or distinguish - which taught the team that simply converting a visual circuit diagram into differently shaped magnets is not sufficient. For Phase 2 they contacted a Beijing school for the visually impaired and visited twice. The first visit was deliberately not a lesson: team members read biology picture books to the children, using a caterpillar's growth to introduce change in living things, while observing how the children used language to describe scientific phenomena and how they responded to different question types. Because the seven participating children were aged 3-8 and had no basis for promoters, terminators or expression regulation, the team stripped the terminology out and kept only the Input-Regulation-Output logic, recast as a 'sound machine': children explored block shapes by touch, assembled the machine, and a volunteer clapped three times as the audio output when it worked. The star block was introduced as the machine's 'good assistant' that makes it run and the X block as the 'bad assistant' that stops it, so activation and repression were learned through immediate auditory feedback. The kit was then donated to the school so teachers can keep using and adapting it for different ages. Third strand: wiki accessibility treated as a deliverable with real user testing. All charts were redrawn in the Okabe-Ito palette and verified against red-green, blue-yellow and total colour-blindness simulations; the page code was rebuilt with semantic tags so screen readers can identify headings, paragraphs and buttons; an accessibility plugin in the lower right corner offers five text sizes with line and character spacing adjusted in step so layout does not break when enlarged, aimed explicitly at elderly readers; and the entire project is translated into Chinese, English and French with two switching paths. The team then invited a person with red-green colour blindness, elderly users and non-native English speakers to test it and iterated on their feedback. Fourth strand: public science communication on neurodegenerative disease, prompted by a survey finding that most junior high school students did not know what neurodegenerative diseases are, associated them only with memory decline in the elderly, or said 'this has nothing to do with me', while high school students had the capacity but no systematic channel; an interview with the local health bureau director in the Guangying area established that medical staff, government and charities are all delivering information but public acceptance is low and prevention habits are not forming, partly because the material is monotonous and dependent on visual text.
good.ihp: The project's human practices thread runs through disease awareness and screening access: interviews with the local health bureau director in the Guangying area on why existing neurodegenerative-disease education fails to land, plus in-school surveys establishing an age-stratified knowledge gap, shaped the public communication strategy to differentiate content depth by audience. The inclusivity work is itself integrated practice - the Chloe Franklin and David Doyle consultations each produced documented, traceable changes to an artefact rather than general encouragement.
good.realWorld: Open outputs: the comparative international laboratory-accessibility legal database, the laboratory accessibility audit tool PDF, the audit evaluation form PDF, the Chinese legal research document, the trilingual accessible wiki itself, and the physical tactile magnetic genetic-circuit kit, which was donated to a Beijing school for the visually impaired for continued teaching use. Commitments are explicit: pilot testing of the audit tool continues into the next season in collaboration with the wider iGEM community.

gemsTakeaway: Build the accessible teaching aid, then pilot it twice: first with sighted participants under blindfold so you catch your own design flaws in a controlled setting, then with the actual users after stripping out the terminology they do not yet have - and donate the finished kit to the partner school so it keeps teaching after you leave.
